answer:
**Short answer:** Based on your lease, you most likely don't have to pay $1,200 while the lease term runs. The lease sets rent at $1,050 and contains nothing that lets the landlord raise it mid-term. It also says it can be changed only by a writing both of you sign, and you haven't signed anything. Chapter 83, part II has no section on rent increases, so the statute doesn't settle this. The lease is the main support for your position. If you pay only $1,050, the landlord might say you underpaid and try to evict you. So you should be careful about that risk.

One thing would help me: before the letter came, had you complained to the landlord, a code or housing office, or a tenant group about the apartment? If so, what was it, and when?

DETAILS

### What does your lease say about the rent?
- Lease §4: "Rent is $1,050.00 per month, due on the first day of each month."
- Lease §3: the term "begins on August 1, 2025 and ends on July 31, 2026." The letter says the new rent starts March 1, 2026, which is within that term.
- Lease §10: "It may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You confirmed nothing was signed.
- The lease has no clause allowing a mid-term increase. I read all of it, and the only clause about staying past July 31 is §9, which is about holding over.
- The statute adds nothing here. Fla. Stat. 83.46(1) says rent is as agreed ("Unless otherwise agreed"). Section 83.46(2) makes a tenancy month to month only if the agreement says nothing about how long it lasts. Your lease has a fixed end date, so that rule doesn't apply.

### Does the law say a landlord can raise rent mid-lease?
- The stored text of part II has no section on notice or limits for rent increases. Fla. Stat. 83.425 also says residential tenancy matters are "preempted to the state," which blocks local rent rules.
- Reading 1: during a fixed term, rent is whatever the lease says. An increase then needs a lease clause or your agreement, and you have neither.
- Reading 2: a landlord who can end a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' notice (Fla. Stat. 83.57(3)) may change the rent the same way. That applies only to month-to-month tenancies, not to yours.
- Reading 3: no particular notice is required at all.
- Nothing in the statute chooses among these. On your facts the lease points to Reading 1.

### What if the landlord tries to collect or evict over the $150 difference?
- If the landlord files an eviction case, you can raise your lease as your defense. You confirmed no case has been filed.
- Fla. Stat. 83.55 lets a party recover "the damages caused by the noncompliance" with the lease or part II. You could rely on this if the landlord's breach of the lease causes you a loss.
- Paying $1,200 under protest is not required, but whether to pay or withhold the $150 is your call. Keep proof of every payment you make.

### Could the increase be retaliation?
- Fla. Stat. 83.64(1) bars a "discriminatory" increase made "primarily because the landlord is retaliating." Under 83.64(4), being treated differently from other tenants is a "prerequisite" to proving it. You must also have acted in good faith.
- Under 83.64(2), retaliation works as a defense once the landlord sues for possession. It is not something you can use before then.
- A complaint before the letter doesn't make the increase retaliatory by itself. Whether other tenants got the same increase also matters. You don't have to know that.

### Why the housing type matters
- Part II doesn't cover some housing, such as residence that is incidental to educational services (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). You confirmed this is a private complex not tied to any school, so part II applies.

### What to keep
- The letter, its date, and how it was delivered: handed to you at the door on February 10, 2026.
- Your lease.
- Proof of each rent payment.

This subsection shall not apply to an employee or a resident manager of an apartment house or an apartment complex when there is a written agreement to the contrary. History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 2, ch. 81-190; s. 2, ch. 87-195; s. 2, ch. 90-133; s. 1, ch. 93-255.

answer:
**Short answer:** Probably yes, your landlord can raise the rent, and this probably isn't retaliation. Florida's retaliation law requires that you be treated differently from other tenants on rent. You told me every unit got the same letter and the same percent increase. The law also doesn't set a notice period for rent increases, so I can't tell you the increase was too late or too early. Retaliation is also only a defense once a landlord sues you for possession of the apartment. Has your landlord filed an eviction case against you or threatened one?

DETAILS

### Can the landlord raise the rent?
- Your lease is month to month (Lease §3). It lists rent of $1,050 (Lease §4). It has no clause on rent increases and none that bars them.
- The lease says it can be changed only by a signed writing (Lease §10). You told me you did not agree to the new rent.
- Part II of Chapter 83 has no section that sets a notice period for a rent increase. I won't give you a number of days.
- The law doesn't settle this, and there are two readings:
  - **Reading 1:** For a month-to-month tenancy, the landlord can change rent on the same notice that can end the tenancy. Fla. Stat. 83.57(3) says "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period." On this reading, the 30-day notice rule applies to the increase.
  - **Reading 2:** No particular notice is required, because no section sets one for increases.
- Local rent rules don't change this. Fla. Stat. 83.425 gives the state control over these matters, and the text I hold has no local rule.
- Facts I have: the letter was handed to you at your door on February 20, 2026. The new rent starts April 1, 2026. Your current monthly period ends March 31, 2026. Lease §8 says notices to you go "to the apartment while Tenant lives there," so hand delivery there fits the lease.

### Is it retaliation?
- Fla. Stat. 83.64(1) makes it unlawful to "discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent... primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant."
- Section 83.64(4) says discrimination means you are "being treated differently as to the rent charged." It calls different treatment "a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct."
- Everyone got the same letter at the same percent. On those facts you were not treated differently, and that weighs strongly against a retaliation claim.
- Your January 20 complaint was a portal repair request about a dripping faucet. Section 83.64(1)(c) protects a complaint to the landlord "pursuant to s. 83.56(1)." That section concerns written notice of a landlord's failure to keep the unit in repair. Whether a portal request counts is something you would need to check.
- You must also have acted in good faith (83.64(1)). Your landlord's motive isn't in the record.
- Even if all that were met, 83.64(2) says retaliation "may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." It also doesn't apply if the landlord proves good cause, such as unpaid rent (83.64(3)).
- The statute may also let a tenant act on a retaliatory increase without waiting for an eviction case. That is unsettled, and I haven't read the damages section (83.55) to check. It would still need different treatment, which you don't appear to have.

### Keep these
- The February 20 letter.
- Your lease.
- Your January 20 portal request.
- Anything showing what other tenants were charged.

answer:
**Short answer:** It may be retaliation, but that isn't settled. Your complaint to code enforcement is the kind of act the law protects, and the increase hit only you. Florida's law, though, requires the increase to be "primarily" because the landlord is retaliating, and nothing yet shows the landlord's reason. Since no eviction case has been filed, you have nothing to raise it against right now. Whether you can act on the increase alone is an open question. You can also end the month-to-month tenancy with written notice instead of paying $1,400. Do you want to stay at a lower rent, or are you willing to move out?

DETAILS

### Does your situation fit the retaliation law?
- The law makes it unlawful to "discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent ... primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)).
- A complaint to a government agency that enforces building, housing, or health codes is one of the listed examples (83.64(1)(a)). You complained to city code enforcement about mold on January 15, 2026.
- The law requires that you "acted in good faith" (83.64(1)). Only you can speak to that. You would need to be able to show the mold complaint was honest.
- The law requires different treatment as "a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct" (83.64(4)). You say your neighbors' rent didn't change. That is what they told you, so it's worth getting proof.
- The landlord's reason is not in the record. The law asks whether retaliation was the primary reason, and the timing alone doesn't prove that.
- The landlord gave you the letter on February 20, 2026, about five weeks after your complaint. I can't say whether that timing helps you.

### Can you use retaliation right now?
The law says it is open on two readings.
- **Defense only.** Section 83.64(2) says retaliation "may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." No eviction case has been filed, so you would have nothing to raise it in yet. The landlord can defeat the defense by proving "good cause," such as unpaid rent or a lease violation (83.64(3)).
- **Unlawful on its own.** Section 83.64(1) calls a retaliatory increase unlawful. Section 83.55 says a party harmed when the other side fails to follow this part "may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance." Under this reading, you could sue for damages. The statute doesn't say which reading is right, and I can't tell you a court would accept the second.

### Was the increase done properly?
- Your lease is month to month (lease §3). It sets rent at $1,050 (§4) and has no clause allowing increases.
- The lease says it "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant" (§10). You say you did not agree to the increase. On that reading, the rent stays $1,050 unless you sign.
- On the other reading, a landlord of a month-to-month tenancy can change terms by ending the tenancy on 30 days' notice. The statute allows that notice "prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- The statute I have contains no section setting a notice period for rent increases, so I can't give you one. Florida law also leaves rent rules to the state, not to cities (83.425).

### Can you leave instead of paying $1,400?
- Yes, if you give written notice of "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Your period ends March 31. Notice to end the tenancy then would have to be given by March 1, 2026, which has not passed.
- If you miss that date, the next period ends April 30. Notice for that would be due by March 31, 2026, which also has not passed. The new rent starts April 1, so the April 30 option would cost you a month at $1,400.
- Your lease requires written notices to the landlord to be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or sent there "by certified mail" (§7). Email doesn't count (§8).

### What to keep
- The February 20 letter.
- Your lease.
- Your code complaint and its date.
- Anything showing what your neighbors pay.

answer:
You may be able to challenge the increase, but the law I have doesn't settle whether the landlord can do it on this notice. The part of Florida law I can see sets no required notice period for a rent increase. Your lease doesn't either. So I can't tell you that two weeks is too short, and I can't tell you it's fine. If you don't want to pay $1,200, you can end your month-to-month tenancy with 30 days' written notice. The last day to deliver that notice for the rent period ending April 30 is March 31, and that date has not passed. Until a court or the landlord settles the question, the safest course is to write to the landlord. Ask which lease clause allows the new rent starting April 1. Also ask to confirm in writing what you owe for April. Before your rent is due, I'd get advice from legal aid or a lawyer on whether to pay the old or the new amount. One question: before this letter, had you complained about the apartment to the landlord or to a city or county office?

DETAILS

### Is a rent increase on this notice allowed?
- The part of Chapter 83 I can read has no section on notice for a rent increase. Your lease doesn't address one either. Clause 4 only says rent is "$1,050.00 per month," and clause 3 makes the tenancy month to month.
- Florida law leaves rent rules to the state. Fla. Stat. 83.425 says the regulation of residential tenancies "and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." I can't apply a city or county rent rule.
- The law doesn't settle this, so there are three readings:
  1. A landlord who may end a month-to-month tenancy on 30 days' notice may change the rent only on that same notice (Fla. Stat. 83.57(3)). On this reading, the April 1 date would be too early.
  2. No section sets any notice for an increase, so no particular notice is needed. On this reading, the April 1 date could stand.
  3. During a fixed term the lease controls. You have no fixed term, so this reading doesn't help you.
- I can't tell you which reading a court would pick.
- Your facts, as you confirmed them, are these. The office handed you the letter at your door on March 20. The new rent is $1,200, starting April 1. You haven't agreed to it, and you haven't paid it.

### Can you leave instead of paying the new rent?
- Yes, because your tenancy is month to month. Fla. Stat. 83.57(3) lets either side end it "by giving not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period."
- The notice must be in writing and delivered in a way Fla. Stat. 83.56(4) names. Those ways are mailing it or handing over a copy. Your lease, clause 7, says notices to the landlord go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or by certified mail to that address.
- For the period ending March 31, the last day for notice was March 1, and that has passed.
- For the period ending April 30, the last day is March 31. That date has not passed.
- A notice delivered by March 31 ends your tenancy on April 30.
- Leaving also brings a second notice. Under Fla. Stat. 83.49(5), unless your lease says otherwise, a tenant who moves out of a month-to-month tenancy gives the landlord 7 days' written notice before leaving. It must go by certified mail or by hand, and it must include an address where you can be reached. Your lease has no clause that changes this. One notice that is in time for both rules and meets both rules' delivery methods covers both. The lease also asks for a forwarding address in writing at move-out (clause 6).
- What you owe for April if you give notice and stay is open for the same reason as the first question. It is $1,050 on the first or second reading and $1,200 on the third.

### Is the increase retaliation?
- It is unlawful for a landlord to "discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent … primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)).
- Retaliation covers things like a complaint to a code enforcement office, a written repair notice to the landlord, or joining a tenant group (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)(a)–(c)).
- You must have acted in good faith (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)).
- You must also be treated differently from other tenants on rent. That is a prerequisite under Fla. Stat. 83.64(4).
- The statute says retaliation "may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(2)). That means that if the landlord sues to evict you, you can raise it. Nothing in the statute I can see says what you can do before a suit, with only an increase.
- There are two readings. One is that the defense works only once the landlord sues. The other is that a retaliatory increase is unlawful by itself, and Fla. Stat. 83.55 lets you recover damages when a landlord doesn't comply with the law.
- The defense also does not apply if the landlord proves the eviction is "for good cause" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(3)). Unpaid rent is an example of good cause.
- The landlord has not filed an eviction case, as far as I know.

### What to keep
- Keep the March 20 letter and note that it was handed to you at the door.
- Keep your lease.
- Keep any earlier complaint you made, with its date.
- Keep anything showing what other tenants were told to pay.

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the landlord has raised the rent or says the rent will go up. It rests on 83.64 (retaliatory conduct), 83.57 (ending a tenancy without a specific term), 83.46 (rent and duration), and 83.425 (preemption).

- The program computes no deadline for this situation: the stored text of Chapter 83, part II has no section on notice of a rent increase. Never state a notice period for rent increases.
- If the tenant wants to end a month-to-month tenancy rather than pay the new rent, lease_ending also covers it, with the steps and the date; load it too.
- The statute leaves some housing out of part II: "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). College housing may be an example. The tool records the facts and does not decide whether this applies; say what the words are and what you would need to know.
- The retaliation rules have an exclusion of their own: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(3)).
- Do not apply a local rent rule from memory. 83.425 preempts local regulation, and the stored text holds none.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- The rent clause: the rent amount in the lease, next to the new rent.
- The renewal clause, and when the lease term began.
- When the lease term ends, next to the date the new rent applies from. Show both and say what the lease says; you do not compare the dates.

### From the tenant

- How much is the monthly rent? (Only if the lease does not show it.) What new rent is the landlord asking for?
- What date did they receive notice of the increase, was it in writing, and from what date does the landlord say the new rent applies?
- Does the lease have a fixed end date (for example, a one-year lease), and what date does the term end? Or is the tenancy month to month (no fixed end date, rent paid monthly)?
- Before the increase, had they complained to anyone about the unit (the landlord, the office, a city or county office), or taken part in a tenant group? If so, what was it, and on what date? Offer the plain choices: a complaint to a city or county office that enforces building, housing, or health codes; taking part in a tenant group; a written notice to the landlord about a repair; another complaint to the landlord (in person, by phone, a portal request); or something else. If more than one fits, take the first in that list.
- What do they know about whether other tenants got the same increase? It is fine if they do not know.
- Has the landlord filed an eviction case in court against them?

### What the deadlines count from

Nothing: the program computes no date for this situation. Do not compare the date of the increase with the lease term yourself, or without the lease's own words.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- The notice of the increase, with its date and how it arrived.
- The lease, especially the rent and renewal clauses.
- Any complaint made before the increase, with its date.
- Anything showing what other tenants were charged.

## What the tenant can do

Tell the tenant first whether they can do each of these and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below). Some conditions are for the tenant to check against what the record shows.

### Raise retaliation as a defense if the landlord sues for possession after raising the rent (Fla. Stat. 83.64(2))

All six conditions must be met. No steps are listed. Whether retaliation can be acted on before any such case is open (the second open question).

1. Before the increase, the tenant did something the statute protects, such as a complaint to a code agency, a written notice to the landlord of a repair the landlord has not made, or joining a tenant organization: "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)). It is met in any of these ways:
   - The tenant complained to a code enforcement office, or took part in a tenant group, as 83.64(1) names. The tenant can tell you. If their step was something else, it is not one of the examples the statute names outright.
   - The tenant gave the landlord a written notice about a repair, which 83.64(1) names when it is a complaint under 83.56(1). The tenant checks whether that notice was one 83.56(1) describes.
   - The statute's examples are not the only conduct it protects. That is not settled (the second open question).
2. The tenant acted in good faith: "In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)). The tenant checks whether the complaint or other step was made in good faith, with what the record shows of it.
3. The tenant is treated differently from other tenants as to the rent: "a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(4)). The tenant checks whether other tenants got the same increase, from what the landlord or other tenants say.
4. The increase was primarily because the landlord is retaliating: "primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)). The landlord's motive is not in the record. That is not settled (the second open question).
5. The landlord has no good cause for the case, such as unpaid rent or a lease violation, which the landlord must prove: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(3)). The tenant checks whether any rent is unpaid or the landlord claims a lease violation.
6. The landlord has brought an action for possession: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(2)). The tenant can tell you. If they say no eviction case has been filed, the defense is raised in a case once one is filed; it is not open yet.

### End a month-to-month tenancy rather than pay the new rent, with written notice at least 30 days before the end of a monthly period (Fla. Stat. 83.57(3))

One condition: the tenancy is month to month. The statute: "When the tenancy is from month to month, by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (Fla. Stat. 83.57(3)). The tenant can tell you, and the lease's term clause shows it. If the tenant says it is not month to month, this option is closed. No steps are listed here, and the program computes no date. Whether an increase may be made, and on what notice, is open (the first open question).

## What the statute does not settle

For each of these, tell the tenant in plain words that the law does not settle it, give every reading and what it would mean for them, and pick none.

### Whether and how a rent increase may be made

The stored text of Chapter 83, part II has no section setting notice for a rent increase. 83.425 says "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (Fla. Stat. 83.425). Set the lease's rent clause beside the increase and, for a tenancy without a fixed term, 83.57. Whether and how an increase may be made is not settled by the stored text; say so plainly with the readings.

- During a fixed term the rent is what the lease says, so an increase needs a lease clause allowing it or the tenant's agreement; part II adds nothing either way.
- For a month-to-month tenancy, a landlord who may end it on 83.57 notice may change the rent on the same notice, "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (Fla. Stat. 83.57(3)).
- For a month-to-month tenancy no particular notice is needed, since no section sets one.

### Retaliation, and what the tenant can do about an increase alone

83.64(1) says "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)). 83.64(4) defines "Discrimination" for that section. Set the record beside its parts: the complaint and its date, what the tenant knows about other tenants' rent, and the tenant's good faith. The landlord's motive is not in the record. What stays open is what the tenant can do about an increase alone.

- 83.64 works only as a defense: 83.64(2) says retaliation "may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(2)), so a tenant facing only an increase has nothing to raise until such an action.
- 83.64(1) makes a discriminatory, retaliatory increase unlawful on its own terms, and 83.55 lets the tenant recover damages when the landlord fails to comply with part II. Fetch 83.55 with get_statute_section before relying on it.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the current rent, the new rent and the date it applies from, the tenant's request, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: Asks the landlord to confirm the new rent, the date it applies from, and which lease provision it rests on. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the lease's rent clause, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.64(1) sentence, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that the program computes no deadline for this situation: the statute text it holds (Chapter 83, part II) has no section on notice of a rent increase. A letter from them does not start any period the program tracks.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period for rent increases. The stored text has none.
- Saying an increase is retaliatory because it followed a complaint. 83.64(1) needs an increase that is discriminatory and "primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)), and 83.64(4) makes different treatment "a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(4)).
- Applying 83.64 without its condition that "the tenant must have acted in good faith" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)).
- Applying a local rent rule from memory. 83.425 preempts local regulation, and the stored text holds none.
- Comparing the increase date with the lease term yourself, or without the lease's own words. The tool compares no dates.
- Computing any date yourself.

# Lease ending

Rests on 83.575 (a set end date), 83.57 and 83.46 (no set end date), 83.58, 83.59, and 83.67 (staying on, no lockout), 83.56 and 83.505 (delivering notices), 83.49 (the 7 days' notice, the deposit), 83.595 and 83.45 (limits on charges), 83.43 and 83.64 (good faith, retaliation), 83.60 (if sued), 83.47, 83.55, and 83.48 (void clauses, damages, attorney fees), and 83.5615 (foreclosure). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets both readings, and you choose neither.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The tenant wants to move out well before the end date: load wants_to_leave_early.
- The landlord's notice names something the tenant did: load notice_received_violation.
- A higher rent comes with the renewal: load rent_increased too.
- After the move, the deposit: load deposit_not_returned.
- A new owner after a foreclosure says to leave: 83.5615 calls for a notice "at least 90 days before the effective date of the notice" (83.5615(2)(a)) and protects a bona fide lease's remaining term, with limits (83.5615(2)(b)). Its note says it takes effect upon the repeal of a federal act, and the stored text does not say whether that has happened; say this needs checking.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the end date; any notice before leaving at the end; any notice from the landlord; any charge for missing a notice; renewal; staying after the end; how notices go; and what move-out requires. Quote each clause and cite it.

A clause that renews the lease if no notice is given: say what it says. Whether option 1's conditions for a charge reach it is not settled. One: it is a way of charging for a missed notice, so the landlord's own notice is needed first. The other: a renewal is not a charge, and 83.575(2) speaks only of liquidated damages, so the clause stands.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date a set term ends. period_end: with no set end date, the last day of the rent period they ask about. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- planned_move_out: the date they plan to leave.
- tenant_notice_delivered: the date their notice reached the landlord, and how it went.
- landlord_notice_delivered: the date a paper from the landlord about the end reached them, how it came, and what it lists. If mailed or left at the door, landlord_notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left.
- permission: what the landlord has said or done about their staying, and whether it is in writing. rent_after_end: any rent paid or taken for a time after the end.
- eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served. complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the landlord acted, and what it was.

## Which kind of tenancy

- **A set end date:** 83.575. Options 1 to 3, and "When the landlord will not renew".
- **No set end date:** 83.57. "If the rental agreement contains no provision as to duration of the tenancy, the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). A home that comes with a job goes by the pay periods (83.46(3)). Option 4, and "When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date".
- **Stayed on with permission after a set term:** read the lease's clause on staying. With none, 83.575(3) points to the 83.57(3) notice; see option 2.

Part II names no right to renew.

## How a notice is delivered

This covers a landlord's notice under 83.575, and either side's notice under 83.57. A tenant's own notice before leaving at the end of a set term goes as the lease says; 83.575(1) names no way for it. The ways: "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- **Handed over:** delivered that day.
- **Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away:** a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. One: the mailing or the leaving is the delivery. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the person. For a landlord's notice, set both landlord_notice_sent and landlord_notice_delivered beside the date. For the tenant's own notice, handing it over or mailing it early meets both.
- **E-mail under the signed addendum:** only with every condition of 83.505(1); then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).
- **A text, a portal message, an e-mail with no addendum, or a copy left at the door while the tenant was home:** not a way 83.56(4) names. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached the person. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice. The other: "This section does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). If there is still time, sending it again by hand or by mail meets both.
- **Spoken:** the statute asks for a written notice in these cases. No notice has been given.

A lease clause on notices adds to this: a way that meets both the clause and the statute is safest. Say what the clause says.

## Option 1: leave at the end of a set term

1. **Does the lease ask for notice?** The lease "may contain a provision requiring the tenant to notify the landlord within a specified period before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement" (83.575(1)). No such clause: the stored text asks for no notice before leaving on the end date. Say so plainly.
2. **Is the clause one the statute allows?** Two limits, each with its own question. Say what is not settled, and that notice by the date given meets both readings.
   - The length: "A rental agreement may not require less than 30 days’ notice or more than 60 days’ notice from either the tenant or the landlord." (83.575(1)). A clause outside it: not settled what follows. One: the statute does not rewrite such a clause, so no notice is owed under it. The other: a clause is void only "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) takes away what part II gives, so it stands at the limit. Over 60 days: the date is count_days(lease_end_date, -60). Under 30 days: count_days(lease_end_date, -30).
   - The landlord's half: the clause must also require "the landlord to notify the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within such notice period if the rental agreement will not be renewed." (83.575(1)). A clause without it: not settled what follows. One: the statute allows the clause only "if such provision also requires" (83.575(1)) that, so no notice is owed under it. The other: the statute does not say the tenant's promise falls away, so it still binds. The date is the lease's own.
3. **The last day.** If the clause gives a number of days N: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If it is in months, give the lease's words; the tool counts days only.

Leaving before the last day of the term: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), a tenant leaving "before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement" (83.49(5)) gives the 7 days' notice: count_days(planned_move_out, -7), in writing, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. Rent through the end date is still owed under the lease.

**What missing the notice costs.** A lease "may provide that if a tenant fails to give the required notice before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, the tenant may be liable for liquidated damages as specified in the rental agreement" (83.575(2)). All of these must be met for that charge:

1. **The tenant missed a required notice.** They gave it in time, or the clause falls under step 2's limits: say so, with step 2's readings.
2. **The lease sets the charge.** No charge in the lease: this part does not apply.
3. **The landlord sent its own written notice first,** "specifying the tenant’s obligations under the notification provision contained in the rental agreement and the date the rental agreement is terminated." (83.575(2)), and it "must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant under this subsection." (83.575(2)). No such notice, or one that leaves any of these out: not met, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.
4. **Delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
5. **In time.** "within 15 days before the start of the notification period contained in the rental agreement." (83.575(2)). The start: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). Fifteen days before it: count_days(lease_end_date, -(N+15)); pass the sum as one number. What the words ask is not settled. One: the notice must come during the 15 days that end when the period starts, not earlier. The other: it must come no later than 15 days before the period starts, and earlier is also in time. Set the date it came beside both dates:
   - On the earlier date: it meets both. Say so plainly.
   - Between the two: it meets only the first reading.
   - Before the earlier date: it meets only the second reading.
   - After the start: it meets neither, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.

The limit on fees for leaving early does not apply here: 83.595(4) "does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (83.595(4)(b)). Do not apply its two months' rent limit or its separate addendum to this charge. Part II sets no number for this charge; a court may refuse or limit an "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) clause, and that is for a court. Apart from this charge, a landlord may claim damages for a failure to follow the lease (83.55); amounts are outside this tool.

Moving out: read what the lease requires. Any claim on the deposit goes through the deposit steps; load deposit_not_returned after the move.

## Option 2: stay on with the landlord's agreement

A new lease or a written agreement says what the rent and the term are. Read the lease's clause on staying and what it requires. "If the tenant remains on the premises with the permission of the landlord after the rental agreement has terminated and fails to give notice required under s. 83.57 (3), the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent." (83.575(3)). So a tenant who stays with permission gives option 4's notice when they leave. Say so. Asking the landlord for its answer in writing settles what permission there is.

## Option 3: stay without permission

Say the risk plainly. A tenant who "holds over and continues in possession of the dwelling unit or any part thereof after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58) can be sued for possession (83.58), and "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). Do not total it. For a tenancy ended by a notice under 83.57, whether it has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. One: a tenancy ended by proper notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of a term, and 83.57 speaks of a tenancy "terminated" (83.57).

But the end date does not put them out by itself: "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)), changing the locks included, and if it does or cuts a utility it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)).

What counts as permission, when the landlord said nothing or took rent for a time after the end, is not settled. One: taking rent for that time is permission, since a landlord that "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (83.56(5)(a)) gives up acting on it. Then 83.58 does not apply, and 83.575(3) and option 4's notice do. The other: permission must be given, and taking rent alone does not change a tenant who holds over, since the same sentence leaves open "any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). Set what the landlord did and any lease clause on consent beside both. Getting the landlord's answer in writing settles it either way.

## Option 4: end a tenancy with no set end date

"A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46 (2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57). No reason is named. The notice, by rent period: year to year, 60 days before the end of the year's period (83.57(1)); quarter to quarter, 30 days (83.57(2)); month to month, "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)); week to week, 7 days (83.57(4)).

1. **The last day.** Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30). If that has passed, the same notice works for the next period: count_days(next_period_end, -30). For another rent period, use its number of days.
2. **Written, and delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
3. **The 7 days' notice too.** "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), it also applies to "any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year" (83.49(5)). It must be written, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address, at least 7 days before leaving: count_days(planned_move_out, -7). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. One notice by hand or certified mail, with the address, in time for both, meets both. Missing it "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)).

A tenant who stayed on with permission after a set term and misses the 83.57(3) notice owes the extra month's rent (83.575(3)). For a tenancy that was month to month from the start, that is not settled. One: (3) names the month-to-month notice, so it applies. The other: the section is about a tenancy "with specific duration" (83.575), so it does not.

## When the landlord will not renew

The tenant has a set end date and the landlord says it will not renew. Part II names no reason it must give.

- **The lease has a notice clause with the landlord's half.** The last day for the landlord: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If the clause is outside the limit, set the notice beside the lease's date and the limit's, as in option 1. If it is in months, give the lease's words. In a named way, on or before the last day: met, and the lease ends on its date. Say so plainly. Late, or not in a named way: what follows is not settled. One: the lease still ends on its date by its own words, and the landlord's miss is a failure of the lease, for damages at most (83.55). The other: the clause makes the landlord's notice the way a lease is not renewed, so without it the landlord cannot hold the tenant to the end date. Say what the lease says about renewal.
- **The lease has no such clause.** The stored text asks for no notice from the landlord before a set term ends. Say so plainly.
- Either way, see option 3 for staying, and "After a complaint" below.

## When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date

Set the landlord's notice beside option 4's rule. Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30), with period_end the last day of the rent period holding the date the notice names. If it was mailed or left at the door, use both dates, as "How a notice is delivered" says.

- **Written, in a named way, on or before that date:** met, and the tenancy ends at period_end. Say so plainly, and go to option 3 for staying.
- **Too late for that period, or naming a date that is not the end of a rent period:** it does not meet the rule for that date. Say so plainly. Whether it works for a later period is not settled. One: it is still written notice, so if it came by count_days(next_period_end, -30) the tenancy can end at next_period_end. The other: it names an end the statute does not allow, so it is not the required notice, and the landlord must give a new one.
- **By text, by portal, or spoken:** see "How a notice is delivered".

Whichever it is, say not to ignore it, and that the landlord still needs a court case (option 3).

## After a complaint

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Not renewing, or giving 83.57's notice, is not named there. Whether either is covered by itself is not settled. One: it is a step toward the action the rule names, so it is covered. The other: the rule lists the landlord's acts, and this is not one.

A tenant sued for possession can raise it as a defense (83.64(2)). The examples of what is protected include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), and a complaint under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), and they are only examples (83.64(1)). The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). They must be treated differently (83.64(4)), and the landlord must have acted primarily to retaliate, which is for a court.

It falls away "if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "violation of the terms of this chapter." (83.64(3)). Whether staying after the end is that kind of violation is not settled. One: holding over without permission is what 83.58 addresses, so it is good cause. The other: that would leave the defense nothing to do whenever a lease has ended. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## If the landlord sues

Say this first when a case has been filed. "In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). A motion needs papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a lease's notice clause binds the tenant without checking the landlord's half and the 30 to 60 days.
- Saying a tenant owes the charge for missing a notice without every condition of 83.575(2), or applying 83.595(4)'s limits to it.
- Saying the tenant must be out on the end date, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case.
- Stating double rent as owed while what the landlord said or did leaves permission in doubt, or applying 83.575(3) with no permission.
- Applying 83.57's 30 days to a set term still running, or treating a late notice as good for the date it names.
- Saying part II gives a right to renew, or requires a reason for not renewing.
- Giving a calendar date for the 5 days in 83.60(2).
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

(3) In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause. answer:
There is no cap in the law I have for this. Chapter 83, part II sets no limit on how much a landlord can raise rent. It also has no section on how much notice a rent increase needs. Part II says the state, not cities or counties, regulates these matters (83.425), so I can't point you to a local rent cap either. Your current lease runs through July 31, 2026, and your rent stays $1,050 until then. The $1,300 applies only to the new 12-month lease that would start August 1, 2026. You haven't agreed to it, so you aren't bound by it.

Your options:
- **Accept the offer.** You would sign the new lease at $1,300.
- **Negotiate.** The law doesn't give you a right to renew, and your landlord doesn't need a reason to decline. You can still ask for a lower rent or a different term.
- **Move out when the lease ends.** Your lease has no clause requiring notice before you leave at the end. You would still need to follow the move-out steps in section 6.
- **Stay without a new lease.** I would avoid staying without your landlord's written consent. Without it, your landlord can sue to remove you and ask for double rent for the days you stay. Your landlord still needs a court case to remove you.

Retaliation is a narrow possibility. Florida law bars a rent increase meant to punish you for something like a code complaint or a written repair request. You could raise it only as a defense if your landlord sues to evict you. It also depends on facts I don't have yet.

Before the offer came, had you complained about the apartment to your landlord or to a city or county office? If so, what was the complaint and on what date?

DETAILS

### Is there a limit on the increase?
- Part II has no section capping rent or setting notice for an increase. The stored text holds none.
- "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (Fla. Stat. 83.425). I haven't applied any local rule.
- Your lease (section 4) sets rent at $1,050.00 a month. Section 3 says the term "ends on July 31, 2026." Your landlord delivered the offer on May 15, 2026, and the new rent would start August 1, 2026.
- Because the new rent starts after the term ends, it is an offer for a new lease. It is not a mid-term increase. During a fixed term, the rent is what the lease says. Part II adds nothing either way.

### Do you have a right to renew?
- Part II names no right to renew. It also names no reason your landlord must give for not renewing.
- Your lease has no renewal clause. Section 9 covers staying past the end: "If Tenant stays after July 31, 2026 with Landlord's written consent, the tenancy becomes month to month on the same terms."
- That clause depends on your landlord giving written consent. Without that consent, the clause doesn't apply.

### What if you leave when the lease ends?
- A lease may require notice before you leave at the end of the term (83.575(1)). Your lease has no such clause, so the stored text asks for no notice from you.
- Section 6 requires you to leave the apartment "clean and empty," return all keys to the office, and give a forwarding address in writing.
- Your landlord must return your deposit under the deposit rules in 83.49, which I can go through after you move.

### What if you stay without a new lease?
- Staying after the lease ends without your landlord's permission can lead to a possession suit. Your landlord may also recover "double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (Fla. Stat. 83.58).
- Your landlord can't just remove you. It "shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except" through a court case, or when you give up or abandon the home (83.59(3)). It also may not lock you out (83.67(2)).
- What counts as permission if your landlord says nothing, or takes rent after July 31, is not settled. One reading is that taking rent is permission. The other is that permission must be given, and taking rent alone doesn't supply it. Getting your landlord's answer in writing settles it either way.

### Could the increase be retaliation?
- The law says: "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant's rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)).
- You must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)). You must also be treated differently from other tenants on rent, which is "a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct" (83.64(4)).
- The law says retaliation "may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(2)). If your landlord hasn't filed an eviction case, there is nothing to raise it in yet.
- Whether you can act on a retaliatory increase before any eviction case is not settled. One reading is that 83.64 works only as a defense. The other is that 83.64(1) makes such an increase unlawful on its own, and 83.55 lets a tenant recover damages when a landlord fails to follow part II.
- The defense doesn't apply if your landlord proves the eviction is for good cause (83.64(3)).

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the landlord has raised the rent or says the rent will go up. It rests on 83.64 (retaliatory conduct), 83.57 (ending a tenancy without a specific term), 83.46 (rent and duration), and 83.425 (preemption).

- The program computes no deadline for this situation: the stored text of Chapter 83, part II has no section on notice of a rent increase. Never state a notice period for rent increases.
- If the tenant wants to end a month-to-month tenancy rather than pay the new rent, lease_ending also covers it, with the steps and the date; load it too.
- The statute leaves some housing out of part II: "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). College housing may be an example. The tool records the facts and does not decide whether this applies; say what the words are and what you would need to know.
- The retaliation rules have an exclusion of their own: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(3)).
- Do not apply a local rent rule from memory. 83.425 preempts local regulation, and the stored text holds none.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- The rent clause: the rent amount in the lease, next to the new rent.
- The renewal clause, and when the lease term began.
- When the lease term ends, next to the date the new rent applies from. Show both and say what the lease says; you do not compare the dates.

### From the tenant

- How much is the monthly rent? (Only if the lease does not show it.) What new rent is the landlord asking for?
- What date did they receive notice of the increase, was it in writing, and from what date does the landlord say the new rent applies?
- Does the lease have a fixed end date (for example, a one-year lease), and what date does the term end? Or is the tenancy month to month (no fixed end date, rent paid monthly)?
- Before the increase, had they complained to anyone about the unit (the landlord, the office, a city or county office), or taken part in a tenant group? If so, what was it, and on what date? Offer the plain choices: a complaint to a city or county office that enforces building, housing, or health codes; taking part in a tenant group; a written notice to the landlord about a repair; another complaint to the landlord (in person, by phone, a portal request); or something else. If more than one fits, take the first in that list.
- What do they know about whether other tenants got the same increase? It is fine if they do not know.
- Has the landlord filed an eviction case in court against them?

### What the deadlines count from

Nothing: the program computes no date for this situation. Do not compare the date of the increase with the lease term yourself, or without the lease's own words.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- The notice of the increase, with its date and how it arrived.
- The lease, especially the rent and renewal clauses.
- Any complaint made before the increase, with its date.
- Anything showing what other tenants were charged.

## What the tenant can do

Tell the tenant first whether they can do each of these and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below). Some conditions are for the tenant to check against what the record shows.

### Raise retaliation as a defense if the landlord sues for possession after raising the rent (Fla. Stat. 83.64(2))

All six conditions must be met. No steps are listed. Whether retaliation can be acted on before any such case is open (the second open question).

1. Before the increase, the tenant did something the statute protects, such as a complaint to a code agency, a written notice to the landlord of a repair the landlord has not made, or joining a tenant organization: "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)). It is met in any of these ways:
   - The tenant complained to a code enforcement office, or took part in a tenant group, as 83.64(1) names. The tenant can tell you. If their step was something else, it is not one of the examples the statute names outright.
   - The tenant gave the landlord a written notice about a repair, which 83.64(1) names when it is a complaint under 83.56(1). The tenant checks whether that notice was one 83.56(1) describes.
   - The statute's examples are not the only conduct it protects. That is not settled (the second open question).
2. The tenant acted in good faith: "In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)). The tenant checks whether the complaint or other step was made in good faith, with what the record shows of it.
3. The tenant is treated differently from other tenants as to the rent: "a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(4)). The tenant checks whether other tenants got the same increase, from what the landlord or other tenants say.
4. The increase was primarily because the landlord is retaliating: "primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)). The landlord's motive is not in the record. That is not settled (the second open question).
5. The landlord has no good cause for the case, such as unpaid rent or a lease violation, which the landlord must prove: "In any event, this section does not apply if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(3)). The tenant checks whether any rent is unpaid or the landlord claims a lease violation.
6. The landlord has brought an action for possession: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(2)). The tenant can tell you. If they say no eviction case has been filed, the defense is raised in a case once one is filed; it is not open yet.

### End a month-to-month tenancy rather than pay the new rent, with written notice at least 30 days before the end of a monthly period (Fla. Stat. 83.57(3))

One condition: the tenancy is month to month. The statute: "When the tenancy is from month to month, by giving not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (Fla. Stat. 83.57(3)). The tenant can tell you, and the lease's term clause shows it. If the tenant says it is not month to month, this option is closed. No steps are listed here, and the program computes no date. Whether an increase may be made, and on what notice, is open (the first open question).

## What the statute does not settle

For each of these, tell the tenant in plain words that the law does not settle it, give every reading and what it would mean for them, and pick none.

### Whether and how a rent increase may be made

The stored text of Chapter 83, part II has no section setting notice for a rent increase. 83.425 says "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (Fla. Stat. 83.425). Set the lease's rent clause beside the increase and, for a tenancy without a fixed term, 83.57. Whether and how an increase may be made is not settled by the stored text; say so plainly with the readings.

- During a fixed term the rent is what the lease says, so an increase needs a lease clause allowing it or the tenant's agreement; part II adds nothing either way.
- For a month-to-month tenancy, a landlord who may end it on 83.57 notice may change the rent on the same notice, "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (Fla. Stat. 83.57(3)).
- For a month-to-month tenancy no particular notice is needed, since no section sets one.

### Retaliation, and what the tenant can do about an increase alone

83.64(1) says "It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)). 83.64(4) defines "Discrimination" for that section. Set the record beside its parts: the complaint and its date, what the tenant knows about other tenants' rent, and the tenant's good faith. The landlord's motive is not in the record. What stays open is what the tenant can do about an increase alone.

- 83.64 works only as a defense: 83.64(2) says retaliation "may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(2)), so a tenant facing only an increase has nothing to raise until such an action.
- 83.64(1) makes a discriminatory, retaliatory increase unlawful on its own terms, and 83.55 lets the tenant recover damages when the landlord fails to comply with part II. Fetch 83.55 with get_statute_section before relying on it.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the current rent, the new rent and the date it applies from, the tenant's request, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: Asks the landlord to confirm the new rent, the date it applies from, and which lease provision it rests on. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the lease's rent clause, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.64(1) sentence, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that the program computes no deadline for this situation: the statute text it holds (Chapter 83, part II) has no section on notice of a rent increase. A letter from them does not start any period the program tracks.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period for rent increases. The stored text has none.
- Saying an increase is retaliatory because it followed a complaint. 83.64(1) needs an increase that is discriminatory and "primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)), and 83.64(4) makes different treatment "a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(4)).
- Applying 83.64 without its condition that "the tenant must have acted in good faith" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)).
- Applying a local rent rule from memory. 83.425 preempts local regulation, and the stored text holds none.
- Comparing the increase date with the lease term yourself, or without the lease's own words. The tool compares no dates.
- Computing any date yourself.
